records.name: Saskatchewan
records.current_summary: In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.  The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.

sources.claim: Government of Saskatchewan education-ministry news release (22 Aug 2023) announcing the parental inclusion and consent policies: schools must seek parent/guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. The release that started the court challenge.

Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (11 Aug 2025): the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision — courts lack jurisdiction to test s.1/s.15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where s.33 was invoked — so the policy stands. Supersedes the injunction-era chambers ruling.

The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that (LGBTQ+ group) UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years. This mainstream coverage independently traces the record's claim that the appeal court largely allowed the government's appeal while keeping the merits challenge alive.

Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The piece corroborates the durable signal this record draws from the case: a consent and name-change rule for transgender pupils shielded from ordinary rights review while litigation continues.

On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause (a five-year override). Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The grant is the key later development for this record: no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

records.name: Scotland
records.current_summary: This region's prosecution system names anti-trans crime as its own charging category: the region's 2021 hate-crime statute created a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation, and the prosecuting authority reported 104 charges carrying it in 2025-26 (up 21% on 86 the year before), while police recorded 8,538 hate crimes in the provision's first full year. For a visitor who is assaulted or harassed, the machinery exists to see the offence counted and charged by name.  The region's parliament also passed a more expansive self-declaration gender-recognition law with a two-thirds majority in December 2022 - evidence of markedly more trans-accepting regional institutions - only for the central government to block it with the first-ever use of a statutory veto order; verification as of September 2026 confirms the bill fell and remains not law, with no revival. The same UK-wide rules on legal sex and single-sex services apply here as across the union state.

sources.claim: COPFS 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26' (30 Jun 2026): 7,115 hate-crime charges total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04; sexual-orientation aggravation 2,062 charges (second commonest category); transgender-identity aggravation 104 charges, up 21% from 86 — the highest since the 2021 Act took effect.

Scottish Government 'Hate crimes recorded by the police in Scotland, 2024-25' (pub. 17 Feb 2026): police recorded 8,538 hate crimes, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh (about 32.25 each); 62% carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator — first annual report under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021.

records.name: Oaxaca
records.current_summary: In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; muxe activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body. These festivals are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.  April 2025 reporting profiles the region as the country's fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation with possible municipal-police participation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, and the state's answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform. The state human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 discrimination investigations involving LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, and violence against muxes persists despite the state's international reputation for diversity.  The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. The result is coexistence: a formally protective legal framework alongside customary exclusion enforced at the exact events tourists attend.

sources.claim: La Tinta Oaxaca (25 May 2024): the organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola 'Lado Sur' festival in Juchitan circulated an invitation stating 'men dressed as women will not be admitted'; muxe activists, incl. defender Felina Santiago (three decades of advocacy), filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body over the transphobic exclusion. Three velas went ahead on 26 May, with muxes affirming they are part of local society and culture.

Trendencias (Apr 2025): profiles Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and simultaneously its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community — violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate; the murdered include muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino (31) and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza (43). State response has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

El Universal (27 Sep 2026): Oaxaca's human-rights ombudsperson (Defensoria) opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022; violence against muxes persists — e.g. muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec, Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

HRW 'Gender Recognition in Mexico by State' (11 Mar 2025), Oaxaca row: the 2019 state civil-code reform created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, extended to age 12+ by decree in 2021, with a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opening the procedure — the documentary layer the summary's 'formally protective framework' claim rests on.

records.name: Tripura
records.current_summary: This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 Bangladeshi nationals including seven transgender people in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to India's financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.  The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve states/UTs to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power. On the audited record there is no statute criminalising trans presence here; the documented harm is police practice at the checkpoints.

sources.claim: Sentinel Assam: Tripura police apprehended 15 Bangladeshi nationals including 7 transgender individuals in separate incidents within 24 hours — bus search at Panisagar checkpoint, North Tripura, on the Assam-Agartala highway; detainees held fake Aadhaar/PAN cards, were en route Mumbai via Guwahati; Tripura shares a 856-km porous border with Bangladesh.

North East Today (2 Aug 2024): at the Panisagar check post, North Tripura district, police detained 7 Bangladeshi nationals — 2 transgender individuals and 5 others described as disguised as third-gender — travelling by bus to Mumbai; case of fraudulent documents and border-crossing routed through the highway checkpoint.

Sentinel Assam (9 Nov 2024): a joint 24-hour operation in Tripura detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people — first group of 6 (3 transgender persons) after midnight destined for Mumbai; second group of 6 with 3 children from Khulna at Udaipur Railway Station; local helper Md Hafizur arrested for facilitating movement.

records.name: Punjab
records.current_summary: In Amritsar — the spiritual centre of the region's dominant faith — Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade at the Rose Garden after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, the faith's highest temporal authority; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason for cancelling the annual event (Washington Blade, 23 April 2025). No other Punjab-specific law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears in the audited sources for this record.  For a trans visitor the documented signal is institutional, not criminal: no statute here targets trans people, but an organised religious authority compelled the cancellation of the region's annual public trans assembly, and the event simply did not happen. Public visibility in Amritsar therefore carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition, and the absence of any recorded state intervention to preserve the event is part of that record.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (never cached; the record URL is malformed - dashes in the date segment where the live site uses slashes - and returns 404); the underlying Washington Blade report (23 April 2025) covers Pride Amritsar cancelling its 27 April 2025 Rose Garden parade after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition.

The national-framework page under which a trans visitor in Punjab (India) stands: on September 6, 2018 the Supreme Court's five-judge bench ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts and holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, while preserving the provision for non-consensual acts; in July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omitted Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which the page says bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. The page carries no Punjab-specific law or institution targeting trans people, consistent with the record's finding that the documented signal in Punjab is institutional rather than criminal.

Wikipedia on India's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab: it was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people, though the page records criticism that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. This protective national framework is the statute a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under and supports the record's statement that no statute in Punjab targets trans people.

records.name: Kerala
records.current_summary: Kerala holds a constituted Transgender Welfare Board — one of the 12 states/UTs reported to the federal parliament in December 2021 as having set one up under the national trans-protection rules (PIB) — and its law-enforcement machinery is measurably engaged: the state registered 2 of the 7 national cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 4 of the 11 recorded in 2023, among the highest sub-national totals in those years (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026).  That activity should be read with the source's own caveat: national recording is sparse (20 cases across 2019–23) because of police registration bias, against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence (2025 Transgender Health study, n=4,964). Registered cases therefore evidence a system that at least accepts complaints, not rarity of violence. No Kerala-specific restriction is documented; for a visitor the picture is one of institutional recognition machinery in a state where such machinery exists and is used.

sources.claim: Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), Kerala rows: 2 of the 7 national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023 (joint-highest with Tamil Nadu) — among the highest sub-national totals, with the report's caveat that national counts are tiny from police-registration bias.

PIB federal reply (Dec 2021): Kerala is among the 12 states/UTs reported to parliament as having constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules — the named-board claim the record summary rests on.

records.name: Assam

Recorded cases prove the complaint system is reachable, not that violence is uncommon.  In the December 2021 federal reply listing the 12 states/UTs that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards (PIB), Assam is not among them — i.e., no state welfare machinery stood in place as of that date. No Assam-specific protective or restrictive statute, ordinance or checkpoint operation is documented in the audited sources; the record supports a thin official-visibility finding balanced against the region-wide caveats, nothing more.

records.name: Ceara
records.current_summary: Ceará is the most consistent lethal hotspot for trans and travesti people in Brazil's Northeast: 11 killings in 2024 — the region's highest toll and third nationally (G1, 28 January 2025, on the ANTRA dossier) — and 8 in 2025, tied with Minas Gerais for the highest state total of that year's 80 nationwide (Igbá Agência, 26 January 2026; SBT News). The 34% national drop is not read as improvement by ANTRA's leadership, since violence reappeared as attempted homicides (at least 75) (SBT News).  There is no state-level legal distinction: the federal constitution and penal code apply uniformly. What sets Ceará apart is sustained lethal exposure, and the national victim profile sharpens it for a visibly trans traveller — 97% of victims are travestis and trans women, over half aged 18–29, 70% of those with recorded race are Black, 97% killed in public spaces with most incidents outside capitals. Two consecutive years at the top of the ranking indicate an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip.

records.name: Paraiba
records.current_summary: Paraíba recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — mid-pack in the ANTRA dossier's state ranking, alongside Paraná, Rio Grande do Norte and São Paulo — within a national total of 80 that still leads the world for the 16th consecutive year (SBT News, 26 January 2026; CNN Brasil). No Paraíba-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly.  The documented signal is therefore exposure, not law: the dossiers' consistent victim profile — young, Black, poor and Northeastern, 97% travestis and trans women, most killings in public spaces at night and outside state capitals, frequently mis-recorded by authorities — concentrates risk on people who present visibly in public. The state's absolute count doubled the best-recorded small-state figure of the same table's lower rows, and sits inside the region the dossiers identify as Brazil's hardest-hit.

sources.claim: SBT News (26 Jan 2026): ANTRA 2025 dossier — Paraíba recorded 4 trans killings in 2025, mid-pack (tied with Paraná, Rio Grande do Norte, São Paulo); Brazil total 80. Supports the record's state tally.

CNN Brasil (2024 dossier): Paraíba recorded 5 trans killings in 2024; Rio Grande do Norte, Acre and Roraima zero; Bahia, Mato Grosso and Pernambuco 8 each. Earlier-year comparison for the record's mid-pack framing.

records.name: Pernambuco
records.current_summary: Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, behind only the two 8-count states in the ANTRA dossier's ranking of that year's 80 national killings (SBT News, 26 January 2026; Valor Internacional). No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was identified in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly.  The dossiers add a geographic caution that cuts against capital-centred assumptions: roughly two-thirds of such killings in Brazil happen in interior cities rather than state capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker (SBT News). A visibly trans visitor in Pernambuco's mid-sized and interior municipalities is therefore in the geography where the recorded danger actually concentrates — alongside a victim profile of young (majority 18–29), overwhelmingly Black (70% of those recorded) travestis and trans women.

sources.claim: SBT News (26 Jan 2026): ANTRA 2025 dossier — Pernambuco recorded 7 trans killings in 2025, behind only the 8-count states (Ceará, Minas Gerais); Brazil total 80. Supports the record's tally.

Diario de Pernambuco, Jan. 27, 2026: Pernambuco was the second Brazilian state with the most killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, with 7 homicides, per the ANTRA dossier released on Jan. 26 — the state's lowest annual count since 2022 (13), after 9 in 2023 and 8 in 2024. The dossier counts 80 trans people killed nationally in 2025, 349 killings across the Northeast from 2017 to 2025, and 83 violent deaths of trans people in Pernambuco over six years, 6th-most in the national ranking for that period. For this record: a Pernambuco-specific confirmation of the state's 2025 total and a year-by-year series showing its repeated high ranking.

G1 Caruaru e Região, Oct. 3, 2025: a trans woman was shot dead inside her home on Oct. 2, 2025 in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste interior of Pernambuco, and the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive, with no arrests reported at publication. The report recalls the national ANTRA count of 122 trans people killed in Brazil in 2024. For this record: a documented 2025 killing outside the Recife capital region, consistent with the dossier finding that most such killings occur in interior municipalities.

Alma Preta, July 7, 2021: Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead on the morning of that day along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe, in the Agreste of Pernambuco, killed by several knife strikes; it was the state's third recorded case of killed trans or travesti people that month. Pernambuco's Civil Police told press the suspect, a 22-year-old known as 'Gaúcho', was lynched by locals at the scene. For this record: a documented interior-state killing of a Black travesti matching the victim profile and geography described in the summary.
